A DAX é uma marca exclusiva da Vilarejo, desenvolvida pela Associação Casa Vip, grupo criado a partir da união de redes especializadas no segmento de acabamentos. A associação reúne cerca de 20 empresas e compartilha experiências de mercado para desenvolver produtos voltados às necessidades observadas no contato com consumidores e profissionais.

A marca está presente em mais de 120 lojas pelo Brasil, levando esse conhecimento compartilhado para soluções destinadas a cozinhas, banheiros e outros ambientes da casa.

articles.summary: Cidade Universitária sediará formação gratuita promovida pelo MEC em novembro voltada para o aprimoramento pedagógico regional.
articles.body:
Cidade Universitária receberá assessoria técnica voltada para a Educação Bilíngue de Surdos — Foto: Arquivo Secom

Macaé foi o único município de toda a Região Sudeste selecionado para receber uma Assessoria Técnica do Instituto Nacional de Educação de Surdos (INES). A capacitação ocorrerá entre os dias 10 e 12 de novembro, das 8h às 17h30, no Auditório do Bloco B da Cidade Universitária. A iniciativa é voltada para professores das redes pública e privada, acadêmicos de licenciatura, a comunidade surda e demais interessados na temática do município e de cidades vizinhas.

A formação tem como foco dois eixos temáticos prioritários: "Libras como L1 - Unidade Curricular" e "Alfabetização e Letramento de Surdos no Ensino Fundamental I". As atividades serão conduzidas por uma equipe composta por dois professores surdos e dois ouvintes, oferecendo uma oportunidade de qualificação especializada para os profissionais de educação e o aprofundamento de estratégias pedagógicas voltadas aos estudantes.

Segundo a coordenação de Educação Bilíngue de Surdos de Macaé, o município está em fase de finalização da minuta que consolida as políticas públicas locais para o setor, e a assessoria técnica do MEC e do INES contribuirá diretamente para fortalecer essas diretrizes na cidade e nos municípios do entorno. A coordenação ressalta ainda que os eixos temáticos foram escolhidos com base nas necessidades reais diagnosticadas na rede de ensino, atendendo a demandas fundamentais da área.

A seleção do município foi oficializada em edital nacional e segue as diretrizes da legislação brasileira para o setor, como a Lei Federal nº 10.436/2002, o Decreto Federal nº 5.626/2005 e a Lei Federal nº 14.191/2021, que reconhece a Educação Bilíngue de Surdos como modalidade da educação básica. O evento é totalmente gratuito e os interessados em participar devem realizar a inscrição previamente por meio do formulário digital oficial disponibilizado pela organização, contando ainda com registro institucional acessível e tradução integral em Libras

articles.title: Assessor de Jair Renan Bolsonaro é investigado por agressão em SC | G1
articles.standfirst: Marcelo Ribeiro Delgado Junior sofreu fraturas no braço e passará por cirurgia. Esposa afirma que garrafa foi arremessada contra crianças durante comemoração da vitória de Lula (PT).
articles.summary: Marcelo Ribeiro Delgado Junior sofreu fraturas no braço e passará por cirurgia. Esposa afirma que garrafa foi arremessada contra crianças durante comemoração da vitória de Lula (PT).
articles.body:
A vítima, Marcelo Ribeiro Delgado Junior, e o homem investigado por agressão, Gustavo Schiphorst — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Reprodução

A esposa de Marcelo Ribeiro Delgado Junior, homem agredido pelo assessor do vereador e deputado federal eleito Jair Renan Bolsonaro ( PL ), afirmou que uma garrafa de vidro arremessada por vizinhos quase atingiu a cabeça do filho de 1 ano do casal.

A agressão ocorreu no domingo (25), em Florianópolis , após a divulgação do resultado das eleições presidenciais. Gustavo Schiphorst é investigado por agredir o próprio primo . O g1 procurou a defesa dele, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, os pais do assessor e um amigo também teriam participado das agressões.

➡️ Jair Renan é filho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro e irmão de Flávio Bolsonaro , que fugiu do Brasil após as eleições de domingo . Neste ano, Jair Renan foi eleito deputado federal por Santa Catarina. Atualmente, é vereador em Balneário Camboriú , onde o Gustavo Schiphorst trabalha como comissionado.

Em nota, a assessoria de Jair Renan informou que aguarda a “elucidação dos fatos de nossa parte e pelas autoridades competentes, para eventuais providências” (veja íntegra abaixo) .

A Polícia Civil informou que o boletim de ocorrência por lesão corporal foi registrado na terça-feira (27) e um inquérito foi instaurado pela 7ª Delegacia de Polícia da Capital para apurar o caso .

Agressão ocorreu após resultado das eleições

Ao g1 , Alícia Garcez contou que a briga começou por volta das 21h30 de domingo, na garagem de casa, no bairro Vargem Grande. A família comemorava a vitória do presidente reeleito Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT).

Segundo ela, os vizinhos, que são parentes do marido, começaram a xingar a família. Em seguida, arremessaram uma garrafa de vidro na direção das crianças que estavam na garagem.

De acordo com Alícia, a garrafa quebrou e quase atingiu a cabeça do filho de 1 ano.

“Eles vieram até a grade, começaram a nos xingar, a proferir palavras ofensivas, xingamentos, e arremessaram uma garrafa de vidro em direção aos meus filhos, que estavam na garagem da minha casa”, relatou.

Diante da situação, Marcelo foi à casa dos parentes para questionar a atitude e pedir o fim das provocações. No entanto, segundo a esposa, ele foi cercado atacado pelos familiares.

Entre os envolvidos estariam Camila Braun Schipthorrst e Michel Schphorrst, pais de Gustavo e tios de Marcelo. Lucas Ferreira Amorim, identificado no boletim de ocorrência como amigo de Gustavo, também teria participado das agressões.

“Ele chegou até eles nesse momento. Eles foram para cima dele, imobilizaram ele, deram chutes na cabeça, deram socos na cabeça, no rosto, e quebraram também o braço dele”, contou.

Após as agressões, parentes levaram Marcelo de carro ao hospital. Alícia relatou que Marcelo sofreu uma fratura grave em três pontos do braço e precisará passar por cirurgia, ainda sem data marcada.

A esposa de Marcelo contou que também foi agredida ao tentar proteger o marido. Ele passou por exame de corpo de delito.

O casal solicitou medidas protetivas contra os três parentes. A Justiça aceitou o pedido na terça-feira (27), com base na Lei Maria da Penha. Os agressores estão proibidos de se aproximar das vítimas e devem manter distância mínima de 200 metros.

Gustavo atua como assessor parlamentar no gabinete de Jair Renan em Balneário Camboriú. De acordo com o Portal da Transparência, ocupa o cargo o comissionado desde 16 de julho deste ano, com remuneração de R$ 4.441,96 e jornada de segunda a sexta-feira, das 13h às 19h.

Ele também é estudante de Administração Pública na Universidade do Estado de Santa Catarina ( Udesc ).

Após o caso repercutir, o Centro de Ciências da Administração e Socioeconômicas (Esag) afirmou que, diante da gravidade dos fatos, o caso será encaminhado às instâncias competentes da Universidade.

"A Udesc esclarece que não antecipa conclusões sobre a responsabilidade individual de pessoas envolvidas em ocorrências externas que estejam sob apuração pelas autoridades competentes. Eventuais medidas disciplinares serão adotadas, quando cabíveis, mediante os procedimentos previstos nas normas da Universidade, assegurados o contraditório e a ampla defesa", disse a instituição.

articles.title: Médica que morreu na Espanha após meia maratona fazia viagem com mãe | G1
articles.standfirst: Oftalmologista estaria animada com a viagem, segundo familiar. Após corrida no domingo (25), não acordou na manhã seguinte.
articles.summary: Oftalmologista estaria animada com a viagem, segundo familiar. Após corrida no domingo (25), não acordou na manhã seguinte.
articles.body:
A oftalmologista gaúcha Victoria d'Azevedo Silveira , de 29 anos, que morreu durante uma viagem à Espanha após participar de uma meia maratona , estava acompanhada da mãe.

Segundo familiares, as duas viajaram juntas para que Victoria disputasse a prova em Valência e, depois, passassem alguns dias de férias pelo país.

Victoria estaria animada com a viagem e comemorava o desempenho obtido na prova, na qual ficou em segundo lugar entre as brasileiras, conforme relatado pela tia.

"Estava feliz e fazendo uma coisa que amava, e acompanhada pela mãe, que era quem ela amava muito", descreve a tia da médica, Zélia Silveira d’Azevedo.

Médica e corredora Victoria d'Azevedo Silveira — Foto: Reprodução/ Redes sociais; Arquivo pessoal

De acordo com Zélia, após concluir a corrida no último domingo (25), Victoria saiu para comer, descansou e, no fim da tarde, seguiu de trem para Barcelona ao lado da mãe. Na manhã seguinte, ela não acordou .

A causa da morte ainda não foi esclarecida. Segundo Zélia, o resultado do exame pericial e informações sobre o translado do corpo não foram divulgados até o fim da tarde de quarta-feira (28).

Médica e corredora Victoria d'Azevedo Silveira — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Médica especialista em glaucoma , Victoria era natural de Porto Alegre e descrita pelos parentes como uma profissional dedicada e apaixonada pela medicina.

Filha única , mantinha uma relação muito próxima com a família, que a define como uma presença marcante e querida por todos ao seu redor.

"Era uma luz na nossa família. Não havia quem não gostasse dela. Estava cheia de planos", conta Zélia.

A ligação com o esporte também fazia parte da rotina da médica. Adepta da corrida há anos, ela seguia uma rotina disciplinada de treinos, alimentação e atividade física. Desde 2020, treinava com a assessoria esportiva Companhia dos Cavalos.

Em nota de pesar, a Companhia escreveu: "Vic, você sempre nos trouxe alegria", "jamais te esqueceremos".

"Vic, você sempre nos trouxe alegria. É exatamente com esse teu sorriso que lembraremos eternamente da nossa Cavalinha.

Fica aqui a homenagem de todos os seus incontáveis Amigos da @ciados.cavalos . Essa equipe que você escolheu e compartilhou momentos incríveis, desde o dia 8 de dezembro de 2020.

Que Deus a receba de braços abertos e possa amenizar toda a dor e a saudade que, junto com a sua família, estamos sentindo pela sua partida.

articles.title: Colisão de trens na Espanha deixa 68 mortos; veja o que se sabe | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro dos Transportes afirma que um dos trens recebeu autorização para retomar a circulação apesar de outro veículo estar parado nos trilhos; governo investiga possíveis falhas de segurança.
articles.summary: Acidente entre dois trens de alta velocidade na Espanha deixou 68 mortos e 80 feridos. Governo investiga falha no sistema de controle ferroviário.
articles.body:
A colisão entre dois trens em alta velocidade na Espanha na última quarta-feira (28) provocou a reação de líderes mundiais e gerou comoção ao redor do mundo. O premiê do país, Pedro Sánchez , prometeu esclarecer as causas do acidente que deixou 68 mortos e 80 feridos .

O ministro dos Transportes, Óscar Puente , afirmou que uma falha no sistema de controle ferroviário levou à interrupção da circulação e que, posteriormente, um dos trens recebeu autorização para voltar a se movimentar, apesar de outro veículo continuar parado nos trilhos.

“Não é aceitável que a Espanha sofra dois acidentes graves com trens de alta velocidade em menos de um ano", afirmou Sánchez. O governo investiga se houve negligência ou falhas nos procedimentos de segurança.

Equipes resgatam vítimas de colisão entre trens de alta velocidade em Urda, na Espanha, no dia 28 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: Javier Soriano/AFP

Quantas pessoas morreram e ficaram feridas?

Ao menos 68 pessoas morreram e 80 ficaram feridas, segundo Ester Padilla, porta-voz do governo regional de Castela-Mancha. As equipes de emergência foram mobilizadas para atender às vítimas e retirar passageiros dos vagões atingidos.

O acidente ocorreu por volta das 8h54 no horário local (3h54 no horário de Brasília), nas proximidades de Urda, a cerca de 140 km ao sul de Madri.

Tudo isso aconteceu em um trecho da linha de alta velocidade que liga a capital espanhola a Sevilha, no sul do país.

Quantas pessoas estavam a bordo dos trens?

O trem da empresa estatal Renfe transportava entre 393 e 397 passageiros, segundo informações divulgadas pelas autoridades. Já o trem da Iryo levava 147 pessoas, incluindo um bebê.

O presidente regional da Andaluzia, Juan Manuel Moreno Bonilla, faz um minuto de silêncio em homenagem às vítimas da colisão entre dois trens de alta velocidade entre as cidades de Mora e Orgaz, na Espanha. — Foto: Marcelo del Pozo / Reuters

De onde vinham os trens e para onde iam?

Os dois trens faziam a rota entre Madri e Sevilha. O da Renfe havia partido da capital espanhola com destino a Sevilha. O veículo da Iryo também seguia nessa rota, mas estava parado nos trilhos quando foi atingido.

O trem da Renfe bateu na traseira do trem da Iryo. O impacto provocou o descarrilhamento de vagões, alguns dos quais caíram em um barranco ao lado da ferrovia.

Passageiros relataram um forte estrondo e um incêndio em um dos vagões.

A causa definitiva ainda não foi esclarecida . Segundo o ministro dos Transportes, o sistema automatizado de gestão de tráfego ferroviário, chamado LZB, parou de funcionar após uma falha de comunicação entre computadores.

Com o sistema fora de operação, o centro de controle ferroviário de Madri assumiu o comando do trecho afetado, de aproximadamente 69 km. Por volta das 8h36 no horário local, o trem da Renfe recebeu autorização para retomar a viagem.

Segundo Puente, a decisão é inexplicável à medida que o trecho continuava ocupado pelo trem da Iryo, que estava parado nos trilhos. Também havia um sinal vermelho impedindo a passagem.

Equipes de resgate trabalham no local da colisão entre dois trens de alta velocidade, entre as cidades de Mora e Orgaz, perto de Toledo, na Espanha, em 28 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Violeta Santos Moura

Ainda não há uma conclusão definitiva sobre a responsabilidade pelo acidente.

Puente afirmou que os protocolos de segurança não permitiam que o trem da Renfe retomasse a circulação normalmente nas condições encontradas. Caso fosse autorizado a seguir, o veículo deveria avançar em velocidade inferior a 40 km/h, procedimento que permitiria ao maquinista parar diante de qualquer obstáculo.

O Sindicato Ferroviário espanhol classificou como prematuro e irresponsável atribuir a colisão a um erro humano antes do encerramento das investigações.

O Ministério dos Transportes espanhol e as autoridades responsáveis pela infraestrutura ferroviária estão apurando as circunstâncias da colisão.

A ADIF, empresa responsável pela infraestrutura ferroviária da Espanha, administra os sistemas de controle do tráfego na região. O ministro Puente apresentou informações preliminares sobre a falha no sistema e a autorização para a retomada da circulação.

Equipes de resgate trabalham no local da colisão entre dois trens de alta velocidade, entre as cidades de Mora e Orgaz, perto de Toledo, na Espanha. — Foto: Ana Beltran / Reuters

Qual era a velocidade do trem no momento da colisão?

A velocidade exata do trem no momento do impacto não foi informada. Segundo o ministro dos Transportes, os trens podem atingir 200 km/h nesse trecho em condições normais de operação.

Em 18 de janeiro deste ano, outro acidente grave ocorreu na mesma linha de alta velocidade , deixando 46 mortos e cerca de 300 feridos.

A nova colisão reacendeu o debate sobre a segurança da infraestrutura ferroviária espanhola. O líder do Partido Popular, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, cobrou explicações sobre as condições dos trilhos, os sistemas de segurança e as medidas adotadas após o acidente anterior.

Equipes resgatam vítimas de colisão entre trens de alta velocidade em Urda, na Espanha, no dia 28 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press/AP

articles.title: Post-SEN support: 'My autistic son and I feel abandoned and failed by the system'
articles.summary: A County Londonderry mother says her autistic son, who has turned 18, "is falling through cracks in the system".
articles.body:
A mother has said she feels her son has been "abandoned and is falling through cracks in the system" because of a lack of support for young adults with learning difficulties.

Cherrise Lanigan's son Callan has autism and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), as well as anxiety and other behavioural issues.

He recently turned 18 but cannot access adult disability services because of the way health trusts assess support needs using an IQ test. Cherisse believes it is a flawed system that is disadvantaging her son.

The Northern Health Trust has said it recognises the approach "can present significant challenges" for individuals and families who do not meet the eligibility criteria.

Cherrise, who lives with her son in Draperstown, County Londonderry, described his autism diagnosis as complex and said that he has "significant social and emotional support needs".

"My son's autism is so much more than his IQ, and he really struggles with the social aspects of being around people, but any help we had has now been taken away because of one test," she told BBC News NI.

"It just feels like he's being treated like he's not that important because without support, he's not going to make progress, so is he just expected to stay at home all his life?"

Callan was diagnosed with autism at the age of two. He was in a special learning unit in a mainstream school for most of his time at school.

He currently attends a further education college with support one day a week but his mother accompanies him to local youth clubs a few nights a week.

"Callan could tell you everything about a computer and how it was built, but he struggles with the social and communication aspects of everyday life," she said.

"But the system just seems to want to put all the emphasis on his IQ and it feels like everything else is less important and because he doesn't fit into a neat box or category, we're left in limbo."

A statement of Special Educational Needs (SEN) ends with school, but in England a care plan is in place until a young person reaches 25.

There have been a number of campaigns in Northern Ireland in recent years to do more for young people with SEN after they leave school.

Health trusts in Northern Ireland use a psychometric assessment to define if someone has a learning disability or not.

An IQ of more than 70 can mean that young people, even those who have previously been assessed as having SEN as a child, cannot access disability services as an adult.

This issue has become particularly acute for many families in Northern Ireland who have a loved one with autism.

Northern Ireland's Independent Autism Reviewer says it is "indefensible" that adults with autism were being left to navigate "the most complex of systems" and as a result are often "left in crisis".

Ema Cubitt said: "Once that learning disability door is closed and that support is taken away, where do these families go?

"Those families who love and support people with the most complex needs are also navigating the most complex systems, and government are well aware of this problem and the issues these families are facing."

Sinn Féin MLA Emma Sheerin has previously raised Callan's case in the Northern Ireland Assembly.

"Callan has just missed that threshold by the tiniest of margins, he has fallen between two stools time and again, leaving him to linger in a wasteland," she said.

"I have previously called on the Department of Health to do something for people like Callan who do not just fit in the box."

She added: "I'm not saying that if Callan had the learning disability diagnosis and access to these services that it would solve everything, but he's being robbed of even being given the chance to try and see if it would help."

The Northern Health and Social Care Trust said it acknowledged the "frustration and worry" felt by Cherisse and Callan Lanigan, but said that it had to commission care through specific mental health and learning disability programmes.

A spokesperson added: "We recognise that this approach can present significant challenges for individuals and families who do not meet the eligibility criteria for accessing these services."

The trust said it would continue to engage with the Lanigan family, and Cherisse confirmed that discussions had started around getting her son more support.

In a statement, the Department of Health said it was aware that young people with autism can present with vulnerabilities similar to those with a learning disability and that further work was needed to meet their needs on a "regional consistent basis".

A department spokesperson added: "Work is underway within a financially-constrained environment to improve clarity, consistency and support for people as they move into adulthood."

articles.title: Tanzania demands for post-poll justice as government accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
articles.summary: Families affected tell the BBC they want answers and financial help as Amnesty says a crackdown continues.
articles.body:
Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured.

"We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC.

On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".

The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded.

Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing.

He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.

Earlier this week, Lissu went on a hunger strike as he was not being allowed access to his lawyers - an allegation the prison authorities denied.

His lawyer Dickson Matata told the BBC on Wednesday he had now been granted a meeting and would be eating again.

In its statement, Amnesty said it had documented how over the past year security agencies had committed human rights violations with impunity against government critics, opposition supporters, media organisations and dissenting members of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party.

"Not a single official has been criminally investigated, let alone prosecuted and punished for the excessive force that Tanzanian security forces used against protesters," said Tigere Chagutah, the group's regional director for East and southern Africa

"In fact, the situation has only deteriorated since the crackdown began. In a classic tactic pulled out of the authoritarian playbook, the authorities are increasingly weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear."

The authorities in the East African nation have repeatedly denied accusations of widespread abuses and say the government is committed to respecting human rights.

Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her.

Last year, the BBC verified multiple videos of police shooting towards protesters. Footage posted online showed demonstrators being confronted by heavily armed units blocking their progress and firing tear gas to disperse crowds.

The BBC has since spoken to families of some of the victims of the electoral violence, who are still seeking answers.

Many, like Mwajuma Hamisi, have been left destitute. Her husband George Kisivani was shot in the northern city of Arusha on 29 October 2025, the day of the vote, and died two days later.

"I lost my husband, upon whom we, a family with five children, depended. We now have no other source of support. I am left to fight for the family on my own. We have no other assistance," the 32-year-old told the BBC.

She now sells vegetables at a nearby market to support the family - and would like help from the government.

Sane, who shot in the leg in Arusha, has been suffering physically and financially.

The father of three says he has undergone more than five major operations to deal with the gunshot wound. He still needs further surgery but says he can no longer afford treatment.

"We have done everything within our means, but we have reached our limit," the 33-year-old told the BBC.

"The government should look into the situation of those of us who have suffered these tragedies, so that we can receive medical treatment, as some of us are still very sick."

He explained how in the wake of the violence hospitals initially refused to treat injured people.

In the intervening months, his relatives have sought help from local officials and the district commissioner, but he says they were told the government had not allocated a budget for victims of the violence.

The BBC has not independently verified his account of those conversations.

A commission of inquiry's report into the violence was handed to President Samia in April, officially recording 518 deaths.

But Amnesty has criticised the fact that the full report has not yet been made public, saying it "entrenches a culture of secrecy".

The president has since set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.

"It is imperative that this new commission comprehensively address the role of security forces in the election-related crackdown," Chagutah said.

The rights group says that between 3 and 17 September 2026, it interviewed 17 people who gave details of a continuing crackdown by the authorities.

Some of them were targeted after demonstrations were called for 7 July to demand democratic reforms and justice for those killed last year.

These marches were banned by the authorities. A 26-year-old man who had expressed support told Amnesty how he was arrested on 24 July in Dar es Salaam and held without charge for 47 days.

He said he was blindfolded by his interrogators who wanted to know who was funding the protests and threatened to kill him.

"On the first day, they didn't give me food. When I asked for water, they urinated on my blindfolded face and said, 'That is the price for those of you opening your mouths to make noise'," he said.

"On the second day, I was taken to Gogoni police station where they beat your legs until they get numb but then insist that you must stand."

The right groups also cites other "acts that may amount to torture... arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances and abductions".

The authorities did not respond to the BBC's or Amnesty's request for comment.

Many of those who lost relatives a year ago want the government to acknowledge their suffering and address their questions about justice, like 40-year-old Neema Munuo.

She says her grief over the death of her 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami, who had gone out to buy phone credit in Arusha when she was shot, has often left her too distraught to leave the house.

"It is a date I will never forget for the rest of my life, because whenever I recall it, I feel as though I am burning inside," Munuo told the BBC.

This feeling resonates with farmer Juma Nasibu, who lives near the city of Mwanza on the shores of Lake Victoria.

He has not seen his 25-year-old nephew Juma Shabani since the unrest.

The young man had been at a cinema hall in the evening when his uncle later heard unconfirmed reports that he was amongst people rounded up and shot. His family have fruitlessly searched for him at hospitals, police stations and prisons.

"To date, what still pains me is that we were never able to recover the body," Nasibu told the BBC.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Healey offers cold comfort' and 'A £100 trick or treat?'
articles.summary: Thursday's papers focus entirely on John Healey's first Budget that included £100 for energy bills and a bank tax.
articles.body:
Chancellor John Healey is on all of the front pages. Both the Financial Times and the Times describe his Budget as "modest" . A senior government figure told the FT the Budget was "not radical, but we don't think the markets would have worn something bigger". Similarly, the Guardian says Healey delivered "a low key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind".

There's a harsher verdict in the Daily Mail . It says the Budget was "a snoozer" . In an editorial the paper says that instead of being a blueprint for national renewal the Budget was a holding statement, putting off every major decision facing the country.

The Daily Telegraph and the Sun say Healey has raised taxes on banks, savers, and landlords, while failing to tackle Britain's ballooning welfare bill. "All the chancellor had to offer was the sound of the cans being kicked down the road," is the Sun's verdict.

On its front page the Daily Express highlights the Conservative leader , Kemi Badenoch's assessment that the Budget was "not bold enough." The paper has also spoken to the former Tory defence secretary, Sir Ben Wallace, who accuses Healey of putting "benefits before bullets".

There's a more positive assessment from the Daily Mirror , which titles its coverage "For the Many, Not the Few". The paper says Healey has unveiled a raft of measures to help cash-strapped families and struggling companies. However the Mirror's columnist, Kevin Maguire, asks if the chancellor could have been braver and more radical, with a bigger tax raid on the banks and oil and gas companies.

The Guardian is one of the papers highlighting Nigel Farage's claim that he was absent from the Commons on Budget day to avoid a "physical altercation" with another MP in a row about seating arrangements. Farage said a green paper slip, saving him a seat, had been removed. The Guardian says that's because the slip wasn't properly stamped with the date.

articles.title: Microsoft profits soar days after announcing thousands of layoffs
articles.summary: The week, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to 60,000 workers as it looks to curb costs.
articles.body:
Technology giant Microsoft says its profits for the three months to the end of September jumped to more than $36.6bn (£27.5bn), just days after announcing plans to cut its workforce by more than a quarter.

On Monday, the Windows developer said it would offer buyouts to around 60,000 of its workers to cut costs as it pours billions of dollars into artificial intelligence (AI).

Like many other major tech firms, Microsoft is investing heavily in the infrastructure that powers AI even as questions remain over whether such huge spending will pay off.

Microsoft shares rose by almost 2.9% in after hours trading in New York on Wednesday.

The recent financial results of tech companies have been closely watched by investors as they gauge whether the heavy spending on AI is sustainable.

Big tech companies like Amazon, Meta and Alphabet are expected to spend more than $700bn this year on AI chips and infrastructure like data centres .

Microsoft said on Wednesday that its quarterly revenue rose to $92.3bn - up 19% from a year earlier - driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business.

Its earnings were lifted by a 30% increase in revenue for Microsoft Cloud - its range of enterprise technology services.

The firm also flagged risks, including "substantial investments" in AI, among other uncertainties that could impact its finances.

The firm's chief executive Satya Nadella said AI development has helped grow the adoption of the technology and has delivered "real-world impact across every industry."

Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know

This week, the company said it would extend a voluntary redundancy offer to eligible employees in teams across Canada, India, the UK and US to adapt its workforce to "changing needs".

It will create "greater flexibility" for the firm and allow workers to leave with financial support and career planning resources, Microsoft said.

The company currently employs more than 220,000 people around the world.

Microsoft's stronger-than-expected earnings contrasted with Alphabet, as the owner of Google disappointed investors with its financial results on Wednesday.

The firm's shares fell by 9.75% after it reported a 25% drop in quarterly net profit from a year earlier and said it will continue to spend heavily on AI.

articles.title: Manhunt grows for escaped murderer who may have left area where truck was ditched
articles.summary: Jacob Morley, who fatally shot a co-worker, escaped Sunday from a prison in Tennessee. The work truck he allegedly stole was found in Illinois.
articles.body:
Jacob Morley, a convicted killer on the loose since Sunday, has no known connection to the small Illinois town where the truck he is accused of stealing was found, the police chief said Wednesday.

"What we have seen kind of leads us in the direction that he's not still here. But that doesn't mean that we've stopped looking," Marion Police Chief David Fitts said.

Morley, 28, convicted of killing a co-worker in 2022 , was serving a life sentence when he escaped from Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, sometime before 11:30 p.m. Sunday, officials there said.

Morley had stolen a work truck, and early Tuesday that truck was found behind a business in Marion, a town of around 16,000 that is around 100 miles north of Tiptonville, authorities in Marion and Tennessee said.

There have been no reports in Marion of any other stolen vehicles, and there was no evidence around the truck that was found, Fitts said.

There have also been no confirmed sightings, he said.

"There's really nowhere for him to go here where he wouldn't be recognized. His face is all over the news," Fitts said.

Morley has no known connection to Marion or southern Illinois, he said.

"Have no idea why he would come here, other than I-57 is a major interstate and it runs right through the middle of our town," Fitts said. "And I don't know, maybe he was low on gas and just pulled off. I don't know."

Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary after a trial in February 2025. He also pleaded guilty to theft of property.

He was accused of shooting Cody Birchfield in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents. Birchfield's body was found in a large metal box under Morley's residence, the documents say.

Birchfield's sister, Carrie Norman, said Wednesday that "it feels like a scary movie."

The family, she said, "have to go back through the experience — once again. Once again, because you don't know where he's at, but you know what he's capable of."

Also Wednesday, the reward for information leading to Morley's arrest increased from $2,500 to $15,000, a combined sum from the Tennessee governor's office, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Marshals Service, the bureau said.

Fitts said he wished Morley had been caught, but he urged people not to take things into their own hands.

"This is really frustrating that we can't find him. Somebody will eventually, I have no doubt in my mind. I wish it was us so we could catch him now," Fitts said. "But, and I just want to let our people know that, again, don't approach him. Call 911. We'll handle it."

Around 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison staff members confirmed that Morley was unaccounted for and conducted an emergency count and search of the facility, the Tennessee Department of Correction said.

Security video showed Morley "breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform," the department said.

The department has not given more details about how the escape occurred, which it said Wednesday is under investigation.

articles.title: The Vatican unveils its holy garage of popemobiles used since 1930
articles.summary: The Vatican is opening a celebration of the popemobile, the now-iconic vehicle that for nearly a century has let popes get close to the faithful at home and abroad.
articles.body: The Vatican is opening a celebration of the popemobile, the now-iconic vehicle that for nearly a century has let popes get close to the faithful at home and abroad. The Vatican Museums on Wednesday unveiled a preview of the exhibition commemorating “A Century of the Popemobile,” featuring eight Mercedes-Benz versions of the car that popes have used since 1930. It officially opens to the public on Thursday. Separately, Pope Leo XIV — a big car lover — met with top Mercedes-Benz executives and thanked them for their partnership with the Holy See. In his remarks, the Chicago-born pope noted that the advances in automotive technology had accompanied the advances and evolutions of papal travel. “Over the decades, the popemobile has evolved from a means of transportation into an instrument of encounter, enabling the pontiff to draw closer to the faithful during pastoral visits and public celebrations,” Leo said. “In this way, your work has helped facilitate the church’s mission of reaching out to people and bringing a message of faith, of hope and of charity to the world.” The oldest car on display in the Vatican Museum exhibit was given to Pope Pius XI on May 23, 1930. The Mercedes-Benz Nürburg 460 featured a luxurious armchair upholstered in silk brocade and finishes of fine wood and metal. It “was specifically built, designed, and prepared for papal use, so much so that just by comparing it, you can see how it transitions from the serial to the unique,” said Sandro Barbagallo, curator of the Historical Collections Department at the Vatican Museums. “From this point, it is clear how all the cars were then made, precisely to allow the pope to be seen, but to be seen and to see in total safety and, I would even say, comfort,” he said. Later versions of the popemobile on view reflected the changing needs of a pope on the road, most importantly his need to engage with the faithful and — more recently — bless babies that were brought to him. In 1960, Pope John XXIII was presented with the 300 d Landaulet, with a detail that foreshadowed change: The removable rear side windows allowed the future saint to reach out to those he met along the way. In 1980, for St. John Paul II’s visit to Germany, Mercedes-Benz developed the 230 G, which featured another major innovation: a tall, transparent dome at the rear, providing safety but also guaranteeing a clear view for the millions of faithful gathered to see him. In his remarks to the Mercedes-Benz executives, Leo recalled the electric popemobile they presented to Pope Francis in keeping with the Argentine pope’s ecological priorities. “In this spirit, I encourage you to continue placing technological innovation at the service of human dignity, care for creation and the common good,” he said.

articles.title: 30-year sentence in Minnesota fraud that drew Trump backlash
articles.summary: Government says Salim Said hit the jackpot in a scheme claiming to feed needy children during the COVID-19 pandemic.
articles.body:
A 37-year-old man who played a key role in defrauding a United States food programme in the state of Minnesota during the COVID-19 pandemic has been sentenced to 30 years in prison, in a case that has drawn intense national scrutiny and political pressure from President Donald Trump.

The widespread scheme in Minnesota, which resulted in dozens of convictions, has repeatedly drawn attacks from Trump, who ridiculed the Democratic governor for failing to stop the scheme and cited it as grounds for an immigration crackdown in the state’s largest cities.

Salim Said, who operated Safari Restaurant in Minneapolis, was accused of vastly overstating the number of meals when seeking payment for providing food to needy children. The government said he was responsible for $44 million in fraud, some of which was committed by others he recruited.

“You took more than taxpayers’ dollars to enrich yourself. You took the reputation of our state down with you,” US District Judge Nancy Brasel said.

Said was claiming a “ridiculous daily distribution of 6,000 meals” while FBI cameras showed 40 people a day collecting food, prosecutors said in a court filing.

“The defendant and his sites did not serve thousands of children; he served a calculated, lucrative lie,” prosecutors said.

Said, who was born in Somalia, denied the allegations while testifying at his 2025 trial, saying many meals were delivered off site. But he changed course and expressed remorse at his sentencing on Wednesday.

Defence lawyer Barry Zone, who had asked for a 12-year prison sentence, disputed the government’s claim that Said was the “architect”.

COVID-19 brought changes to a federal programme that typically fed children through schools. Restaurants could participate, and food distribution was extended to places outside schools.

“For 21 consecutive months, Said made thousands of fraudulent reimbursement claims,” prosecutors said. “Each submission represented meals purportedly provided to underprivileged children, yet the listed children themselves were entirely fictitious.”

The government said Said hit the jackpot, using the stolen funds to buy a $1.2 million home, commercial real estate and an $87,000 pickup truck.

Said was convicted in 2025 alongside Aimee Bock, leader of the Minnesota nonprofit Feeding Our Future, who is serving a 42-year prison sentence for devising the scheme and was ordered to repay $242 million.

State auditors found that Minnesota’s education department received numerous complaints about Feeding Our Future but often told the group to police itself. Following relentless criticism from Trump over theft in federally funded programmes, Governor Tim Walz announced in January that he would not run for re-election.

Former Minnesota state Senator Scott Jensen, left, and former Republican candidate for lieutenant governor Matt Birk speak at a news conference at the State Capitol in St Paul, Minnesota, attacking Democratic Governor Tim Walz over his administration’s handling of an investigation into the nonprofit Feeding Our Future, on September 26, 2022 [File: Steve Karnowski/AP]

articles.title: US Health Secretary RFK Jr to expand access to unapproved peptides
articles.summary: Health experts have cautioned against use of the drugs, citing a lack of clinical trials for humans and the unknown long-term effects.
articles.body:
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. has released plans to loosen restrictions on controversial peptides.

The plans, which were announced in the US Federal Register on Wednesday, say Kennedy would allow compounding pharmacies to prepare six popular peptides, which not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

In an unusual move, the draft came from the office of the health secretary rather than the FDA. After the plan has been officially published later this week, there will be a two-week public comment period.

Unregulated injectable peptides have become popular online. Experts have warned of their lack of clinical trials for humans and unknown long-term effects.

US health panel loosens restrictions for controversial peptides popular online

The peptides mentioned in the plan include BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c and Semax. Compounding pharmacies will be able to mix them to create medications.

The BBC has contacted the FDA for comment.

An FDA advisory panel voted in July to loosen restrictions on the six peptides. But FDA staff members recommended against it.

Kennedy has described himself as a "big fan" of the drugs and has previously vowed to ease restrictions on them after the Biden administration clamped down on the growing industry.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids, or small proteins, which our bodies naturally produce. They act as messengers, telling cells what to do, and play vital roles in skin health, immune system and hormone regulation.

Peptides have been used to treat medical conditions for more than a century. Insulin, one of the first peptide hormones to be discovered, helps people with Type 1 diabetes and some with Type 2 manage their blood sugar levels.

But now unregulated peptides have exploded onto the wellness market since GLP-1s, weight loss drugs, became mainstream.

Online influencers have been marketing peptides in what they have called "stacks" for unproven uses, claiming they can be used as a quick way to help people look younger, heal or improve their skin.

They have become popular among teens on TikTok, especially boys, over unproven claims they help to build muscle, part of online trends known as "biohacking" and "looksmaxxing".

Health experts have cautioned against use of the drugs, citing a lack of clinical trials for humans and the unknown long-term effects of the substances.

articles.title: Activists accuse Israeli settlers of assault in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Footage shows men, some armed, beating a US journalist and an Israeli-Russian activist in Umm al-Khair.
articles.body:
Russian activist Adele Shoko has said that Israeli settlers attacked her alongside two of her colleagues in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, in the Masafer Yatta area of the occupied West Bank, according to social media posts.

Shoko said on social media platform X that she, US journalist Jasper Nathaniel, and Israeli-Russian activist Andrey X were beaten and threatened by armed settlers who stole equipment and personal items.

“Jasper and I were also beaten. Jasper was then pepper-sprayed and arrested,” Shoko wrote, adding that Nathaniel was taken away by Israeli forces.

Shoko said Andrey X suffered a concussion and lost consciousness multiple times during the incident before being detained by authorities.

“Andrey was severely beaten and lost consciousness several times in front of police. Despite this, he was denied hospital treatment. He was put in an ambulance – but instead of being taken to hospital, he was taken to a police station. He is still there, arrested and being denied medical care,” she wrote.

Video footage Shoko posted online showed several men, some of them armed, beating Nathaniel and Andrey X. Further video showed Israeli authorities leading away Nathaniel while he shouted that he had just been beaten up.

The assault follows an October 16 incident in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, where masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, setting trees on fire and throwing stones using slingshots.

Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was covering the attack, was beaten, robbed, and hospitalised, while a Palestinian man was shot in the leg by Israeli soldiers who arrived on the scene and fired live ammunition and tear gas.

Levine, who was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS”, said settlers repeatedly kicked and beat her on the ground before stealing her passport, phone, and camera equipment. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray condemned the “unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job”, while several US lawmakers called for an investigation and an end to settler violence in the region.

articles.title: Alvin K. Hellerstein, federal judge who presided over Trump, Maduro and 9/11 cases, dies at 92
articles.summary: Just two weeks ago, Hellerstein presided over the arraignment of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife on torture charges.
articles.body: Alvin K. Hellerstein, a Manhattan federal judge who presided over cases involving President Donald Trump, former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the 9/11 attacks during nearly three decades on the bench, has died. He was 92. Hellerstein died Wednesday morning while surrounded by his family, Chief Judge Laura Taylor Swain said in a statement. His funeral is scheduled for Thursday at Riverside Memorial Chapel in Manhattan. Swain remembered Hellerstein as a “distinguished jurist” and praised his “energetic and dedicated service” to the court, which continued until his death. “He is greatly appreciated and will be sorely missed,” she said. Just two weeks ago, Hellerstein presided over the arraignment of Maduro and Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, on torture charges that were added to their ongoing narco-terrorism conspiracy case. Maduro, who was captured alongside his wife in January in a surprise U.S. military raid in Caracas, twice defied Hellerstein’s request to enter a plea. Irked, Hellerstein took matters into his own hands, interjecting that “a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro.” At Flores’ Oct. 8 bail hearing, Hellerstein coughed and struggled to speak at times, telling lawyers: “I have a voice problem. As long as you can understand — hear me, I’ll keep going.” Nevertheless, he was resolute that he’d preside over Maduro and Flores’ trial, which he’d scheduled for next June. “We were saddened to learn of Judge Hellerstein’s passing and offer our condolences to his family,” Maduro's lawyer, Barry Pollack, said. Analisa Torres, the judge taking over the case, was part of an international monitoring delegation for Venezuela’s 2006 presidential election, won by Maduro’s late mentor and predecessor, Hugo Chávez. A federal judge since 2013, she previously served on the state bench in Manhattan. A New York native and Columbia Law School graduate, Hellerstein served in the U.S. Army Judge Advocate General’s Corps and worked as a Manhattan litigator before President Bill Clinton appointed him to the federal bench in 1998. He kept a robust docket even after moving to senior status in 2011. Rulings left Trump’s conviction in place In August, in one of his last significant rulings, Hellerstein again spurned Trump’s effort to erase his hush money conviction, rejecting the president’s bid to move the case to federal court and have it dismissed on presidential immunity grounds. “Paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity,” Hellerstein wrote, referring to the $130,000 payoff to adult film actor Stormy Daniels at the heart of Trump’s case. It was the third time Hellerstein had denied Trump’s requests to move the case. The first time was after Trump’s March 2023 indictment; the second followed Trump’s May 2024 conviction and a subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling that presidents and former presidents cannot be prosecuted for official acts. Hellerstein revisited the matter after the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that he erred by failing to consider “important issues relevant” to Trump’s request. The panel expressed “no view” on how Hellerstein should rule. In 2020, Hellerstein sprang Trump’s estranged former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen from prison after the Justice Department revoked his home confinement to thwart his efforts to publish a book or talk to the media. The government’s action, he ruled, was retaliatory and a First Amendment violation. ‘This is different. This is 9/11.’ In the aftermath of the 2001 attack on the World Trade Center, Hellerstein presided over dozens of wrongful death, injury and property damage lawsuits — a two-decade-long effort that shaped his legacy on the bench. Some of the judge’s former clients died in the attack and, lawyers say, he showed great empathy to victims and their families, meeting with them for hours in his chambers and rejecting what he felt were low-ball settlement offers. In March 2010, Hellerstein rejected a proposed settlement that would have paid at least $575 million to thousands of people who fell ill working in the toxic ash of the trade center. He acknowledged he was breaking with tradition by getting so involved. “Most settlements are private. A plaintiff and defendant come together, shake hands and it’s done with,” he said. The judge usually has no part in saying yes or no. “This is different,” Hellerstein said. “This is 9/11.” Others were dismayed when, in 2008, Hellerstein ended an effort to force New York City government to keep searching for human remains in debris moved from ground zero to a Staten Island landfill. High-profile cases until the end Hellerstein's other notable cases included the criminal trials of Charlie Javice, who was convicted last year of defrauding JPMorgan Chase out of $175 million by exaggerating the customer base for her financial aid startup, and hedge fund founder Bill Hwang, who was convicted in 2024 of securities and market manipulation fraud in a scheme that cost banks billions of dollars. He also presided over a 2025 civil trial at which a jury ordered French bank BNP Paribas to pay nearly $21 million for giving the Sudanese government access to the U.S. financial system as it engaged in atrocities two decades ago. In 2015, Hellerstein ordered a New York City cable company to pay a Texas woman $229,500 for flooding her phone with 153 robocalls. Hellerstein, known for a quirky independent streak and strict discipline in his courtroom, insisted spectators wear pandemic-era masks for years after other judges stopped the practice. He “lived a life of commitment to public service and devotion to his community,” the court said in a statement. “His example and work ethic will continue to be a model for this court.”

articles.title: Neighbours: AI micro-drama recut of Australian show focusing on Margot Robbie worries actors and crew
articles.summary: A micro-drama will use AI-assisted technology to edit old episodes of the Australian TV soap to focus on Margot Robbie's character.
articles.body:
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.

Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.

Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.

Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.

Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.

In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".

The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.

"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".

The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.

Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.

"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.

Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.

That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.

Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.

"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.

"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."

Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.

Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".

"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".

Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".

The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.

The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.

It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.

The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.

"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

articles.title: Some North Korean workers sent to Russia are helping Ukraine war effort, report says
articles.summary: Undercover investigators found that workers had been hired at production sites, including a military rations factory, as part of a scheme funding North Korea’s weapons programs.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — A Russian network of brokers sponsored by Pyongyang has taken North Koreans to work in Russia in exploitative conditions and in violation of U.N. sanctions, some at factories that turn out items Moscow uses in the Ukraine war, a rights group said. The neighbors have greatly strengthened military and political ties since pledging renewed cooperation at a 2023 summit of their leaders, while a mutual defense pact is a cornerstone of a partnership treaty signed the following year. In its report, the Hague-based group, Global Rights Compliance (GRC), said North Korea reaps funds from the operation, taking much of the wages earned by its workers who are sent to Russia and made to stay under threat of retribution. The group cites open-source information on the operation run by a Russian businessman, facial recognition technology to identify North Korean officials, and evidence gathered by its members posing undercover as prospective employers. “This investigation exposes a dangerous convergence between two states’ military ambitions,” said the group’s legal adviser, Elise Lauriot Prevost. These were “North Korea’s use of overseas forced labor to finance its weapons program, and Russia’s growing reliance on labor to sustain its war economy,” she added. Russia’s foreign ministry and the North Korean Embassy in Moscow did not respond to emails seeking comment. The rights group said it contacted two Russians identified as key figures in the network, but only one replied, denying the accusation. It did not say whether the other responded. Since 2024, North Korea has sent more than 10,000 troops to fight alongside Russians in the Ukraine war, as well as weapons to replenish Moscow’s dwindling armory while gaining valuable battlefield experience, South Korea’s intelligence agency has said. To evade U.N. sanctions that ban member nations from hiring North Korean workers, the latter enter Russia on student visas in the guise of enrolling at colleges, GRC said. Then they are contracted out to Russian employers, with brokers receiving a commission of up to 150,000 rubles ($1,860) for each, it added. GRC investigators posed undercover as prospective employers and found the workers were hired at production sites, including a military rations factory. The workers are forced to stay on the job through coercion and threats of retribution against them and their families. One advertisement assured prospective employers that workers would not “run away,” the report said. Workers labor 12-hour days with two days off each month, it added, citing such ads. After North Korea’s sixth and last nuclear test in 2017, a U.N. Security Council resolution put a blanket ban on the hiring of its workers overseas and mandated their return home. Russia and China, two permanent members of the Security Council that voted for the ban, have since been accused by South Korea and the West of noncompliance with resolutions. Such measures, dating back to 2006, banned the flow of goods, energy, weapons and workers with North Korea. In previous years, Russia employed North Korean laborers in its far east while many North Koreans staffing restaurants in China sent home wages that were channeled to the state treasury, rights groups have said. North Korea is directly involved in running the network supplying workers in Russia, with officials from its Moscow embassy identified as inspecting work sites for prospective employment, the GRC report said. “These workers do not come cheap, yet little, if any, of the money paid for their labor reaches them,” said Dylan Carter, a GRC lead investigator. “Instead, it lines the pockets of the DPRK state,” he added, referring to North Korea by a short version of its official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

articles.title: ‘We have run down our stock of missiles’: Obama asks 'how is this war going' - watch
articles.summary: Former US president Barack Obama has renewed his criticism of president Donald Trump’s war against Iran, saying the conflict has depleted US missile
articles.body: Former US president Barack Obama has renewed his criticism of president Donald Trump’s war against Iran, saying the conflict has depleted US missile stocks, left American forces and allies vulnerable to attacks. Obama further alleged that the war has also given Tehran leverage over the Strait of Hormuz.Speaking at a campaign rally in Morrow, near Atlanta, Georgia, on Wednesday, Obama questioned the costs and strategic consequences of the war as both leaders campaigned ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.“How is this war going? Our allies and bases have been attacked. Americans have been killed. Hundreds of Americans have been wounded,” Obama said.“We have run down our stock of missiles, making us more vulnerable, and Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where much of the world's oil goes through to get to consumers,” he added.Obama also linked the conflict to rising oil prices, saying, “This is the reason why the price of oil is up.”His latest remarks followed an earlier attack on the war in Ohio, where Obama told Democratic supporters that the conflict had given Iran “veto power” over the Strait of Hormuz. He has also challenged Trump’s rationale for military action, arguing that diplomacy had previously constrained Tehran’s nuclear programme.“I didn’t have to fire any missiles. I engaged in diplomacy,” Obama said, referring to the 2015 nuclear agreement negotiated under his administration. He argued that the deal had curbed Iran’s nuclear activities.Trump, when asked about the war earlier on Wednesday, defended his approach and left open the possibility of further military action or a negotiated settlement.“I've done it very effectively and I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win,” Trump said.Obama, campaigning for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces Republican Representative Mike Collins in Georgia, also framed the midterm contest as a question of American values.“There is a moral component to the choices we face right now,” he said, invoking the legacy of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who is buried in Atlanta.“We are not going to fix the system that's broken, we're not going to unrig our economy, so long as we've got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it's OK to lie and cheat and bully, if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure of our worth,” Obama added.Trump, meanwhile, campaigned in Chillicothe, Ohio, alongside Republican Senator Jon Husted, who faces former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. The president attacked Brown over immigration, saying of Springfield, Ohio, which received Haitian migrants: “The town went to hell.”Trump also faced protesters during the rally. Responding to a heckler who raised the issue of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, he said: “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago.”Neither Trump nor Obama is on the ballot, but both are campaigning to influence congressional races. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are being contested, with Democrats seeking to take control of the House and narrow the Republicans’ 53-47 Senate majority.With voting already under way and about 40 million ballots cast, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, the Iran war, energy costs and control of Congress are set to remain central issues as voters head to the polls.You use AI every day. articles.title: Part of Brighton’s 160-year-old West Pier collapses into the sea during Storm Austen as Victorian landmark continues to deteriorate after decades of storm and fire damage
articles.summary: Part of Brighton’s West Pier collapsed into the sea on Friday, October 23, as Storm Austen brought strong winds to southern England.
articles.body: Part of Brighton’s West Pier collapsed into the sea on Friday, October 23, as Storm Austen brought strong winds to southern England. The Victorian structure, which opened in 1866, has been deteriorating for decades. It closed in 1975, lost sections during storms in 2002 and suffered two devastating arson attacks in 2003. The West Pier Trust describes the remains as being in a state of active collapse and warns that the structure is dangerous and should not be approached. A second storm, Boelo, brought further disruption across the UK over the weekend of October 24 and 25, including power cuts, transport problems and the deaths of two men in separate incidents involving falling trees.A Victorian landmark shaped by storms, fire and decades of declineThe West Pier was designed by engineer Eugenius Birch and opened in 1866. It became a prominent feature of Brighton’s seafront before closing completely in 1975 because of safety concerns. Sections of the structure were lost to storms in 2002, followed by two arson attacks in 2003 that caused extensive damage. The pier is Grade I listed, reflecting its architectural and historic significance. However, its exposed position and continuing deterioration have left much of the structure beyond conventional restoration. A section fell into the sea on October 23 as Storm Austen passed the south coast, according to the Associated Press. The agency quoted historian Fred Grey describing how the pier had been gradually eroded by natural forces since the 2003 fires.The Met Office’s observations for midnight to midday on Friday, October 23, recorded a maximum gust of 76 mph at St Mary’s Airport in the Isles of Scilly and 74 mph at Aberporth in Wales. These readings cover that specific period rather than the full duration of Storm Austen. The storm also affected electricity supplies. The Associated Press reported that more than 31,000 homes in southwest England remained without power by mid-afternoon, citing National Grid. Engineers had restored power to more than 52,000 properties since the storm began, a separate cumulative figure.Why the West Pier cannot simply be stabilisedThe West Pier Trust says the remains have been in a state of active collapse for three decades. Its official website warns visitors that the structure is dangerous and should not be approached. The Trust also says it has no funds to maintain the ruin in a stable condition and that stabilisation is not technically feasible. In a statement reported by local outlet ImJustBrighton, the Trust’s honorary historian described stabilising the remains as too dangerous and costly. The structure is therefore expected to continue changing as sections deteriorate and fall away. The Trust has also described the possibility that the remains could eventually form an offshore reef visible at low tide. The pier’s condition illustrates the challenges involved in preserving historic structures exposed to the sea. Its listed status recognises its heritage value, but that designation does not remove the practical and engineering difficulties of maintaining a severely damaged structure in an exposed marine environment.Storm Boelo brings further disruption across the UKStorm Boelo followed Storm Austen, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to northern parts of the UK over the weekend of October 24 and 25. In its October 22 forecast, the Met Office issued a Yellow wind warning covering the whole of mainland Scotland, the Western Isles, Orkney and the far north of England. The warning was in force from 6 pm on Saturday, October 24, until 9 pm on Sunday, October 25. The forecast warned of widespread gusts of 55 to 65 mph, with speeds of 70 to 80 mph possible in more exposed coastal locations. Subsequent warnings were upgraded in some areas as the storm approached. The Met Office recorded a maximum gust of 84 mph at Machrihanish in Argyll and Bute and 82 mph on the Isle of Tiree, according to STV News.Two men died after trees fell during Storm Boelo on Sunday, October 25. One was a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland. The other was a man in his 20s who died after a tree struck his car in north London, according to reports. The storms also disrupted electricity supplies and transport. The Energy Networks Association reported that 838,700 UK properties had been affected by power cuts across Storms Austen and Boelo combined. Network Rail warned of major disruption to rail journeys in northwest England on Sunday, October 25, after heavy rain flooded tracks and strong winds brought down overhead power lines in several locations. The successive storms highlighted how high winds and heavy rainfall can affect infrastructure, transport networks and historic sites in different parts of the country. For coastal structures such as the West Pier, the effects of severe weather add to damage accumulated over many years.What research says about climate risks to historic coastal sitesResearch published in Nature Communications in 2018 examined climate-related risks to 49 cultural World Heritage sites in the Mediterranean region. The study found that 37 sites were exposed to flood risk and 42 to coastal erosion, using the base year 2000 for its assessment. Under the study’s high-end sea-level-rise scenario, defined by the 95th percentile of Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5 (RCP8.5), the regional mean flood-risk index rose from 3.7 to 5.5, an increase of almost 50%. The regional mean coastal-erosion risk index increased by 13% by 2100 under the same scenario.The research did not examine Brighton’s West Pier, and its figures should not be applied directly to the structure. It nevertheless provides wider context for the risks facing coastal heritage sites as sea levels rise and erosion continues. Individual sites face different combinations of exposure, structural condition, historical damage and available resources for conservation. For the West Pier, the immediate issue remains the management of a historic ruin that continues to deteriorate. The Trust advises visitors to keep away from the structure as its condition changes.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: North Korea fires around 10 ballistic missiles toward sea off east coast, Seoul says
articles.summary: North Korea last fired ballistic missiles on Oct. 12 amid heightened tension on the inter-Korean border over a mine blast that wounded South Korean soldiers last month.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea off its east coast on Thursday, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said. The missiles were launched around 12:30 p.m. local time (11:30 p.m. Wednesday ET) from an area around Wonsan on North Korea’s eastern coast, the JCS said in a statement. South Korea’s military was strengthening surveillance and maintaining readiness in case of additional launches, while closely sharing information with the United States and Japan, it added. Japan’s Defense Ministry said North Korea had launched an object that could be a ballistic missile and that it fell outside Japan’s Exclusive Economic Zone, according to the Yonhap news agency. Japan’s coast guard also said earlier that the launched projectile could be a ballistic missile and had already fallen into the sea. North Korea last fired ballistic missiles on Oct. 12, amid heightened tension on the inter-Korean border over a mine blast that wounded South Korean soldiers last month. Pyongyang has conducted missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year.

articles.title: Why Is the Moon Worshipped on Karwa Chauth? The Hidden Spiritual Meaning Behind the Ritual
articles.summary: A woman stands on her terrace after a full day without food or water.
articles.body: A woman stands on her terrace after a full day without food or water. She lifts a sieve, waits for a pale disc to clear the rooftops and pours water towards it. To an outsider it looks like a simple custom. But every part of this moment rests on ideas that run deep in Vedic thought, astrology and the Puranas.Moon as the Ruler of the MindThe Vedas call the Moon the lord of the mind. A well-known line from the Purusha Sukta says the Moon was born from the mind of the cosmic being. Vedic astrology follows the same principle and names Chandra as Manas Karaka, the significator of emotions, thoughts and inner peace.Marriage survives on the strength of the mind. Love fades without patience, and trust breaks when the mind turns restless. So when a wife prays to the Moon, she is really praying for a calm, steady emotional bond in the home.A strong Chandra in a chart gives tolerance and care. A weak one brings mood swings and misunderstandings. The Karwa Chauth arghya is meant to strengthen this very planet for both partners.The Moon as Soma, the Giver of LifeIn Vedic texts, Chandra is also Soma. He holds amrit, the nectar that feeds herbs, crops and every living being. That is why the Moon is linked with long life and good health.This connection explains the purpose of the fast. The vrat is kept for the husband’s longevity, and the Moon is the planet that carries the essence of life in Vedic belief. The offering of water completes the link. Chandra rules the water element in astrology, and the karwa itself is a vessel of water. When water from the karwa is poured towards the Moon, it returns life-giving energy to its source and asks for its blessing in return.Shiva, the Moon and RenewalLord Shiva wears the crescent Moon on his head, which gives him the name Chandrashekhar. The Puranas tell how Chandra was cursed by Daksha Prajapati to waste away. Shiva gave him shelter, and the curse eased into the monthly cycle of waning and waxing that continues to this day.This story holds a quiet message for married couples. Every relationship has phases. There are weeks of distance and weeks of closeness. And like the Moon, a bond that seems to be waning can come back to fullness with faith and care.Karwa Chauth occurs in Krishna Paksha which is when the Moon is in its waning phase and is slowly decreasing . Worshipping it at this stage is a reminder that love must be protected even when it is not at its brightest.The Meaning of the SieveThe chalni is one of the most striking parts of the ritual. The wife first sees the Moon through it and then her husband’s face.Spiritually, the sieve stands for filtering. It separates the fine from the coarse. Looking through it is a symbolic act of letting go of the year’s complaints and small hurts, and keeping only what is pure in the relationship. The same gaze that is offered to the divine Moon is then turned to the husband. This places the partner in a position of respect, almost like a deity, for that one moment.There is also a link to the Veervati story. Her brothers used a sieve to create a false Moon, and she broke her fast too soon. Using the chalni today is a way of honouring the real Moon and correcting that old mistake.Fasting and the Lunar RhythmThe Moon governs the fluids of the body, which is why lunar days have always guided Indian fasting. A nirjala vrat that ends at moonrise ties the body’s discipline directly to Chandra. Withdrawing from food and water through the day turns attention inward. By evening, the mind is quieter and more focused, which is the state in which prayer is believed to carry the most weight.So the Karwa Chauth Moon is far more than a signal to break the fast. It represents the mind, the nectar of life and the cycle of renewal. Each of these is something a marriage needs to last.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.
