articles.title: Can Turkiye’s Libya breakthrough reshape Eastern Mediterranean diplomacy?
articles.summary: Ankara wins backing from former adversaries in Libya for maritime border agreement, but other diplomatic tests remain.
articles.body:
Istanbul, Turkiye – Once adversaries, Turkiye and the leadership of eastern Libya are now building closer political and military ties. Ankara has also repaired relations with Egypt in the past few years after previous hostility, but a maritime dispute is testing how far those reconciliations can go.

On Wednesday, Turkiye’s Ministry of National Defence renewed its offer to sign a maritime boundary agreement with Cairo, arguing that Egypt could gain more than 15,000sq km (5,790sq miles) of maritime jurisdiction – a figure that is Ankara’s estimate – compared with a potential further agreement with Greece, with which Cairo signed a partial maritime deal in 2020.

The offer came eight days after Libya’s eastern-based parliament in Tobruk reversed years of opposition and approved a maritime agreement signed between its rival, the internationally recognised government based in the Libyan capital, Tripoli, and Turkiye in 2019.

The agreement delineates maritime jurisdiction areas claimed by Turkiye and Libya in the Mediterranean, but Greece, Cyprus and Egypt argued that it infringes on their sovereign rights while Turkiye maintains that it complies with international law.

A senior Turkish official told Al Jazeera that eastern Libya’s leaders had come to recognise Ankara’s intentions.

“Turkiye is not there to use Libya for its own purposes,” the official said.

“From the very beginning, we have supported a policy of one Libya,” the official added, stressing that the country’s stability and resources should benefit all Libyans.

Turkiye helped repel a 2019-2020 offensive on Tripoli by forces loyal to renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, leader of the military forces of the eastern government. Ankara has since expanded its relations with the eastern camp while maintaining ties with Tripoli.

The senior official said Turkish security personnel based in Tripoli had remained in contact with eastern Libyan forces even during the confrontation.

“There has actually been no change in our policy. Only the results it has produced have changed,” the official said.

The diplomatic outreach has been accompanied by military and intelligence contacts.

In May, Defence Minister Yasar Guler met Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son, and Abdulsalam al-Zoubi, a senior defence official in the Tripoli-based government.

Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin also met Saddam Haftar in Benghazi on June 23. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan followed in August, meeting both Khalifa and Saddam Haftar.

A change in Libya’s eastern parliamentary leadership also preceded the maritime vote. On October 6, lawmakers replaced Aguila Saleh as parliament speaker with Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi, who previously chaired the Libyan-Turkish parliamentary friendship committee.

Galip Dalay, a senior research fellow at Chatham House, sees Ankara’s engagement with its former adversaries as a strategic gain.

“This is not merely a pragmatic or tactical gain. It is a strategic gain for Turkiye,” he told Al Jazeera.

Dalay argued that closer relations with both Libyan camps make it harder to establish Eastern Mediterranean energy and security arrangements that exclude Turkiye.

The rapprochement also reflects political calculations within the Haftar camp.

Tarek Megerisi, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Saddam Haftar hopes Ankara’s influence could strengthen his own political prospects with many believing that he eventually wants to lead Libya.

The senior Turkish official said Ankara had made no specific political commitments to eastern Libyan officials beyond general principles and cooperation that would also benefit Libya.

Representatives of both Libyan camps held talks in Ankara on Friday about unifying their military structures, according to Libyan media reports. Differences over political oversight remain unresolved, and no final agreement has been announced.

But Anas El Gomati, director of the Sadeq Institute, cautioned that an understanding between Libya’s rival leaders would not necessarily produce an inclusive political settlement.

“An elite bargain between two camps can leave out everyone beyond them,” he said.

The Libyan eastern parliament’s reversal has also complicated Egypt’s position. Cairo has traditionally supported the eastern leadership but opposes the maritime agreement it has now endorsed.

On October 22, Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis announced discussions with Egypt on extending their partial 2020 maritime delimitation agreement eastwards towards Cyprus.

Four days later, Egypt joined Greece, Cyprus, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union in a statement at the United Nations rejecting the Turkiye-Libya accord.

Yet Cairo and Ankara have continued rebuilding their relationship.

Turkiye’s land forces commander, General Metin Tokel, arrived in Egypt on Monday for an official visit. The Turkish Defence Ministry has also announced a joint naval exercise in Alexandria from November 4 to 9.

The senior Turkish official told Al Jazeera that Ankara remained open to cooperation on maritime boundaries and energy but would defend what it considers its rights.

“Just as other countries say they will not give up the rights they recognise as their own, the same applies to Turkiye,” the official said.

Fidan has acknowledged Egypt’s concerns and discussed the possibility of cooperation with Italy. The official clarified, however, that no formal four-country negotiating mechanism between Turkiye, Libya, Italy and Egypt has been established.

El Gomati believes Cairo’s ability to influence decisions in eastern Libya has diminished.

“Egypt still has influence, but it no longer has a veto,” he said.

Megerisi, meanwhile, argued that Turkiye’s relationship with Egypt has become too important to sacrifice over the maritime dispute. He sees room for accommodation, potentially involving Italy’s energy company Eni, which has interests in Egypt and Libya.

Greece maintains that the maritime agreement disregards the rights of its islands, including Crete. Turkiye rejects those claims, arguing that islands should not automatically receive the same weight as mainland coastlines when mapping out maritime boundaries and exclusive economic zones.

Megerisi said the eastern Libyan parliament’s approval strengthens the agreement’s domestic legal footing but does little to resolve the wider dispute between the countries of the Eastern Mediterranean.

“I think both sides are maximalist,” he said.

The parliamentary vote gives Ankara greater political leverage, but it does not settle competing maritime claims or clear the way for offshore energy exploration.

Ankara now wants to build on its gains in Libya and improving ties with Egypt to strengthen its position in the Eastern Mediterranean. Its aim is to develop new partnerships and regional cooperation rather than remain outside arrangements shaped largely by Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

But that will require finding common ground with countries that continue to challenge Turkiye’s maritime claims.

The senior Turkish official said Ankara’s improved relationship with Cairo had opened the door to discussing those differences directly.

“We can now discuss every issue with Egypt, and we will discuss this one too,” the official said. “We do not have to seek the approval or consent of unrelated third countries.”

articles.title: An Australian couple bought five acres to build a fairytale castle and put their wedding on hold; 22 years and 100,000 bricks later, the 27-room project is still unfinished, with only three of eight turrets complete
articles.summary: An Australian couple who decided to get married only after completing their dream home have been waiting for their wedding for 22 years.
articles.body: An Australian couple who decided to get married only after completing their dream home have been waiting for their wedding for 22 years. Christina Kent and her partner Francis Shepherd bought five acres of land near Geeveston in Tasmania to build a fairytale castle themselves. More than two decades later, their unusual home, called Castle Phoenix, has 27 rooms, stands 17 metres tall and has used around 100,000 bricks. However, construction is still underway, with just three of the eight planned turrets completed. The couple has continued working on the property despite financial difficulties, health problems and years of demanding construction work.According to ABC Australia, their story began in Queensland, where Christina met Francis through a motel owner while teaching an art lesson. Francis worked as a tiler and sculptor, and he wanted to build a castle inspired by the kind of buildings he had admired for years. Christina was interested in his idea, and their relationship developed quickly. Within three weeks of meeting, they were engaged.The opportunity to turn that idea into reality came two years later. During a visit to Christina's niece in Tasmania, they found a five-acre property outside Geeveston. It had a small cottage, an apple orchard and enough space for the large home Francis wanted to build. The asking price was just over A$200,000. They bought the land and moved into the cottage while preparing for construction.Francis began working on designs for a large home with several floors and tall turrets. The couple sought professional help to prepare the plans and applied for permission to build. This was when they also decided their wedding would take place once the castle was finished. At the time, they could not have known how long the project would continue.How couple turned their idea into a projectThe first challenge was getting permission for such an unusual building. According to the official Castle Phoenix website, the proposed height was considerably greater than the normal eight-metre limit in the area. The couple wanted a structure reaching 17 metres.Their application received council approval in late 2009, and building permission followed in 2010. However, they still had to find the money and carry out much of the construction themselves.Christina sold her house in Mackay, Queensland, and the couple arranged a small loan. Francis continued working as a tiler, with Christina assisting him, so they could earn money for the project. Their own construction work took place around those jobs, including during evenings and weekends.The early stages involved preparing the land and creating the underground sections of the building. Work on the sculpture garden began in January 2010, while excavation for the castle followed later that year.Progress was slow because the structure required extensive groundwork. The couple spent several years building the basement before the upper walls began taking shape.Their official construction records show that by early 2012, six basement rooms had concrete floors with underfloor heating. Work on staircases, arches, walls and other sections continued over the following years.What makes Castle Phoenix different Castle Phoenix is not simply a large house with towers. Christina and Francis have treated the building as an art project, creating many of its decorative features themselves.According to Christina's account published in Australian magazine That's Life!, the couple have used around 100,000 bricks, cutting them into approximately 300,000 pieces during construction.The building also has a basement extending three metres underground. Christina said the structure already weighs around 600 tonnes.Inside, the couple has created unusual rooms and decorations. One underground space has a rounded design that causes sounds to echo. Another contains a tree sculpture with handmade leaves.The entrance area has hundreds of ceramic flowers made by the couple. They have also used colourful mosaic tiles across different parts of the property.Outside, the grounds contain a sculpture garden, flowering plants, a lake and a moat. A balcony inspired by the fairytale character Rapunzel is another feature of the castle.Years of construction brought challengesWorking on such a large project has not been easy for the couple. Christina said they had faced financial pressure and health problems while trying to continue construction.However, they have not worked entirely alone. Francis' mother Hope, his sister Veronica and several friends have helped with decorative features, particularly mosaics in the gardens.Over time, the castle also began attracting attention. Christina started sharing updates on Facebook in 2012, and people outside Tasmania gradually learnt about the project.According to her, visitors from Germany, the United States and the United Kingdom have approached the couple for tours.The couple have also considered what should happen to the property in the future. Christina said they would like the public to enjoy Castle Phoenix after they are gone.When will the wedding take place?Although much of the castle has been built, several major parts remain unfinished. Francis began working on its conical rooftops in 2023, but only three of the eight planned turrets have been completed. Christina said exterior tiling was continuing, while the couple hoped to install the windows in 2027.Their wedding, meanwhile, remains on hold. In her account to that's life!, Christina recalled their decision to wait until the castle was complete. "We said we'd get married when the castle was finished; that was 22 years ago! Lucky I like long engagements!" she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Why a Democratic win in US midterms could adversely affect Europe
articles.summary: Complacency about rising far-right movements and renewed pressure on Ukraine could be the result.
articles.body:
The United States midterm elections appear stacked against the ruling Republicans, with polls suggesting the Democrats average an eight-point lead in the House of Representatives and the Senate. But if Democrats take one or both houses, could they affect upcoming elections in Europe?

Not fundamentally, analysts and observers have told Al Jazeera, but besides a welcome improvement in transatlantic relations, they point to two potentially adverse effects.

First, a Democratic Congress might produce complacency among Europeans regarding their own far-right movements.

Second, it might spur US President Donald Trump to raise pressure on Ukraine to make a deal it doesn’t want to make with Russia.

“If the Democrats win the House, let alone both houses, it will be read as, ‘you see democracies bounce back,’” said Catherine Fieschi, a nonresident scholar at Carnegie Europe, specialising in European far-right politics. It would introduce “the idea that these things don’t mean the advent of a fascist regime”, she said.

From her vantage point in Paris, Fieschi said she imagines a Democratic win leading to “a whole discussion about whether we should fear a Marine Le Pen election as much as some people say we should, or whether, in fact, it’s swings and roundabouts and, at some point, if people are really bad and really incompetent, then elections right the way,” she said.

French right-wing politician Marine Le Pen is currently leading the field in polling for presidential elections scheduled for April 18, with surveys indicating she has about 34 percent of the popular vote.

There is a precedent for the complacency Fieschi alludes to. In June 2025, the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), a think tank, polled Europeans following Trump’s first six months in office. Clear majorities in Western Europe said the US political system was broken. In Eastern Europe, majorities said it was working well – though they were weighted towards right-wing voters.

Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris warned against giving too much credit to the US for what Europeans think and do, however.

He said he believes European public opinion hardened against asylum and economic migration independently, but the US marked the shift by expressing it more violently, with military deportation flights and armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents sweeping American cities.

“I think there was a European about-turn on migration. We saw this in Germany, which had a welcoming attitude [to refugees] for many years, and they went to a more controlled policy. All northern European governments saw societies change,” he told Al Jazeera.

“But the US provided a change in tone, from induction and integration and benefaction to deterrence, border protection, increased returns and consequences if asylum is denied. I do think that pivot played a role in Europe,” Plevris added.

Should French voters decide that the only way out is through electing Le Pen – “like some kind of strong medicine that would wake us up to what we might lose”, as Fieschi put it – they would have to contend with three controversial propositions – cutting French financial contributions to the European Union’s federal budget to pay for earlier retirement, cutting military aid to Ukraine and possibly leaving the single currency, the euro, in favour of a devalued franc.

Any one of those policy moves would be a major setback for the European project, which has coalesced around trade, money and now security. A cut in assistance to Ukraine would remove 3.5 percent of its foreign military aid, according to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine Support Tracker , which other allies would have to make up.

At the same time, “we could end up in a situation where Trump is basically clinching deals with Putin as fast as he can,” said Fieschi, referring to the US-Russian strategy to coerce Ukraine into a peace agreement that involves sacrificing its eastern Donbas region – something Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said would be a strategic error leading to renewed war, and which a majority of Ukrainians are against.

Trump has already leveraged US early warning on incoming ballistics and Starlink satellite navigation against Ukraine. He has twice echoed Russian calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced.

Compounding this renewed pressure from a beleaguered White House, Russia could intensify its “all-domain war”, which many European governments believe it is already waging against them, said Victoria Vdovychenko, a Ukraine expert at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.

“Cognitive warfare never stopped on the European continent, and Russians are already using existing vulnerabilities to the utmost,” she told Al Jazeera. “I hope that the European partners will be staying very strong.”

Trump’s abandonment of the world order the US and Europe established after World War II, his disregard for democracy and human rights, and his betrayal of Ukraine have already transformed European public opinion, observers say.

Only 31 percent of Europeans see the US as Europe’s “most trustworthy ally”, down from 51 percent in 2024, when Trump’s predecessor, Joe Biden, was in office, according to a poll for the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung.

Seventy-three percent of Europeans across all age groups say Europe should “go its own way” rather than continue a close cooperation with the US, up from 63 percent in 2024, and that figure includes a clear majority among those on the centre-right and right.

In this year’s Spring Eurobarometer, a regular pulse-taking conducted by the European Commission, 68 percent of respondents wanted the EU’s role in protecting Europeans from global crises and security risks to increase, while 39 percent wanted it to be a top priority.

In a June poll for the European Council on Foreign Relations, the description of the US as an “ally” fell from 22 percent in November 2024 to 11 percent across all territories polled in Eastern and Western Europe.

In a June poll for the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based think tank, 76 percent of people polled in 36 countries, of which nine were EU members, expressed no confidence in Trump, and 57 percent expressed unfavourable views of the US.

It would appear that such shifts against the US and especially Republicans, formed over two Trump terms, would be difficult to reverse in a single congressional election, especially with a Russian war ongoing in Europe.
